title: Winter storms
summary: Know what the National Weather Service alerts mean, get ready before the storm and stay off the roads. Shovel slowly. Never touch a fallen power line. If you’re stranded in a car, stay with it, keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow, and run the engine and heater about 10 minutes each hour with one window slightly open, only while everyone in the car is awake: turn it off before anyone sleeps.
doFirst: Stranded in your car? Stay in it (National Weather Service). Clear snow from the exhaust pipe, then run the engine and heater about 10 minutes each hour with one window slightly open. Everyone in the car stays awake while the engine runs; turn it off before anyone sleeps (National Weather Service, CDC, Red Cross; Carbon monoxide protocol).
Never touch a fallen power line (CDC).
Blizzard or Winter Storm Warning: don’t travel, or delay your trip until conditions improve. If you must travel, carry a winter survival kit (National Weather Service).
Heart disease or high blood pressure? Follow your doctor’s advice about shoveling. Everyone else: dress warmly and work slowly (CDC).

list: Nor’easter: a storm along the East Coast, most frequent and most violent between September and April. Nor’easters nearly always bring heavy rain or snow and gale-force winds, and sometimes coastal flooding (National Weather Service).

Lake-effect snow: cold air, often from Canada, crosses the open water of the Great Lakes and builds narrow bands that can drop 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) of snow an hour or more. Heavy snow can fall in one place while the sun shines a mile or two (2 to 3 km) away (National Weather Service). The bands can bring sudden drops in visibility (National Weather Service).

Ice storm: freezing rain coats roads, walkways, trees and power lines with ice. Enough ice makes travel dangerous or impossible and is likely to snap power lines and bring down tree branches (National Weather Service).

Blizzard: frequent gusts of 35 mph (56 km/h) or more with falling or blowing snow, frequently cutting visibility to under 1/4 mile (400 m) for three hours or more. Whiteouts make travel extremely difficult (National Weather Service).
Snow squall: a short burst of moderate to heavy snow with gusty winds, low visibility and whiteouts, dangerous for drivers (National Weather Service, New York State definitions).

blocks.p: Warnings: take action. Watches: be prepared. Advisories: be aware (National Weather Service).

head: Alert
What the National Weather Service says
rows: Conditions are favorable for a significant winter storm: heavy sleet, heavy snow, ice storm, heavy snow and blowing snow, or a mix. Its occurrence, location and timing are still uncertain.
A significant winter storm with snow, ice, sleet or blowing snow. Travel will become difficult or impossible in some places. Delay travel until conditions improve.
Severe winter weather is expected or occurring, with whiteouts. Do not travel. If you get stranded, stay with your vehicle.
Ice accumulation that will make travel dangerous or impossible and likely snap power lines and bring down branches. Travel is strongly discouraged.
Lake-effect snow squalls or heavy showers are expected to bring significant snowfall, with sudden drops in visibility.
Advance notice of a short, intense burst of snow with gusty winds and whiteouts. Sent as a phone alert when squalls pose a substantial threat to travel.
Snow, blowing snow, ice or sleet is expected but below warning level. Expect winter driving conditions and use caution.

blocks.p: From about October 1, 2026, a Blizzard or Ice Storm Warning may say Particularly Dangerous Situation. That means high confidence of a storm of extreme and historic severity, an exceptional threat beyond a typical blizzard or ice storm (National Weather Service).
Cold alerts (Extreme Cold Warning, Extreme Cold Watch, Cold Weather Advisory) are in Wind chill and cold danger.

list: Stock your home, workplace and vehicles with the supplies you might need. At home, the main worries are losing heat, power and phone service, and running short if the storm lasts more than a day (National Weather Service).
Refuel heating fuel before you run out: fuel carriers may not reach you for days after a winter storm (National Weather Service).
Have a battery-powered NOAA Weather Radio or other radio, a flashlight and extra batteries (National Weather Service).
Make sure your carbon monoxide alarm works and the outside vents are clear; clear them of snow during and after the storm (National Weather Service).

Winterize the vehicle before the season. Before a trip, fill all fluids, check the lights, heater and wipers, and keep the gas tank near full to avoid ice in the tank and fuel lines (National Weather Service).
Bring pets inside or move animals to sheltered areas, with water that isn’t frozen (National Weather Service, CDC).
Stay indoors as much as you can and keep trips outside short (CDC).

As soon as it is safe to go out, make sure snowdrifts aren’t blocking a gas furnace’s vent. If an upstairs gas furnace vents out the roof, you may need to turn it off until the snow melts off the roof (National Weather Service).
Any fireplace, wood stove or space heater: use fire safeguards and ventilate it properly (National Weather Service). Read its topic first.
Keep steps and walkways as free of ice as you can with rock salt, another de-icer or sand (CDC).

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: Sheltering in your house or another building with the heat out: pick one small room and close it off. See Stay warm when the heat is out.

blocks.label: Stay warm when the heat is out

blocks.p: Caught outside with no shelter nearby: build a lean-to, windbreak or snow cave to get out of the wind. From time to time, move your arms, legs, fingers and toes vigorously to keep blood moving (National Weather Service).

list: Avoid travel if you can (CDC, New York State). Don’t travel in low visibility, and avoid ice-covered roads, overpasses and bridges if at all possible (CDC).
Before you go, clear all ice and snow from the vehicle, tell someone where you are going and your route, and take a fully charged phone, a car charger and an emergency kit (National Weather Service).
Snowplows travel at up to 35 mph (56 km/h). Never pass a plow while it is working; stay well behind it, where the road is clear and salted (New York State).
Never pour water on the windshield to clear ice or snow: it can shatter the glass (CDC).

blocks.warn: Stay with the vehicle. Don’t try to walk in a winter storm: you can easily get lost in blowing and drifting snow, and staying in your car lowers the risk of frostbite and raises the chance of rescue (National Weather Service). Leave only if help is visible within 100 yards (91 m) (Red Cross).

steps: Make the car easy to see: tie a brightly colored cloth (red is best) to the antenna, and raise the hood once snow stops falling (CDC, Red Cross, National Weather Service).
Clear snow from the exhaust pipe before you run the engine, and keep it clear, to lower the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning (National Weather Service, CDC, Red Cross).
Run the engine and heater for about 10 minutes each hour, with one window slightly open for fresh air, the downwind one if you can (National Weather Service, CDC, Red Cross).

Everyone in the car must be awake whenever the engine runs: wake anyone asleep before you start it, and turn it off before anyone goes back to sleep. Never run an engine in a vehicle where people are sleeping (Carbon monoxide protocol). If more than one person is in the car, take turns sleeping (Red Cross), only while the engine is off, so someone is always awake.
At night, turn on the dome light while the engine runs, so you can be seen (National Weather Service, Red Cross).
Move anything you need from the trunk into the passenger area. Wrap your whole body, including your head, in extra clothing, blankets or newspapers. Huddle with others for warmth (CDC).

Keep moving your arms and legs as you sit (CDC). Stay awake as much as you can: you will be less vulnerable to cold-related health problems (CDC). If you must sleep, sleep in turns with the engine off (Red Cross; Carbon monoxide protocol).
For light, use a flashlight, not a candle (the app’s choice, D51; the Red Cross and CPSC say flashlights, not candles, at home in an outage). Don’t eat snow: it lowers your body temperature (CDC).

blocks.warn: Don’t rely on the car for heat: it could break down (CDC). If anyone in the car gets a headache, dizziness, drowsiness or confusion, think carbon monoxide: open it up to fresh air and open the protocol.

list: Cold weather puts extra strain on the heart. If you have heart disease or high blood pressure, follow your doctor’s advice about shoveling snow or other hard work in the cold (CDC). The same goes for breathing problems such as asthma (New York State Department of Health).
Otherwise, dress warmly and work slowly so you don’t sweat too much. Your body is already working hard just to stay warm, so don’t overdo it (CDC).
Avoid overexertion: shoveling heavy snow, pushing a vehicle or walking in deep snow. The strain of the cold and hard work may cause a heart attack (Red Cross).
Stretch before you go out, and cover your mouth to protect your lungs from very cold air (Red Cross).

sections.h: Downed lines and after the storm

blocks.warn: Heavy snow and ice can bring down power lines and cause gas leaks. Both can be deadly but are not obvious at first glance (National Weather Service). Never touch a fallen power line, and never drive through standing water with downed lines in it (CDC).

list: Never touch anything or anyone in contact with a power line: you could be shocked through the line, an object or the person (National Weather Service La Crosse).
A live wire on the ground spreads electricity through the ground around it, so you can be shocked near it (National Weather Service La Crosse). Keep away.

A line falls on your vehicle: stay inside and warn others to keep away. Wait inside until rescuers arrive, and don’t touch metal parts of the vehicle. Call 911 if you can (National Weather Service La Crosse).
If fire or other danger forces you out, jump clear so you never touch the vehicle and the ground at the same time. Don’t run: hop away with your feet together (National Weather Service La Crosse).
Check your home, and check on family and neighbors who live alone (National Weather Service).
Melting snow can flood roads, and creeks and rivers often overflow. Avoid flooded roads (National Weather Service).
Partly cleared roads may be icy or blocked. Watch for black ice and potholes (National Weather Service).
Walking on ice is extremely dangerous: many cold-weather injuries come from falls on icy sidewalks, steps, driveways and porches (CDC).
